content: Sucking lice, scientifically classified under the suborder Anoplura, consist of approximately 500 species. They represent the smaller of the two traditional suborders of lice. All members of Anoplura are obligate blood-feeding ectoparasites that exclusively parasitize mammals. These parasites are capable of causing localized skin irritations and can act as vectors for the transmission of various blood-borne diseases. Children appear to be particularly prone to lice infestations, potentially due to the finer texture of their hair, which may facilitate the attachment and movement of lice. Among the Anoplura, at least three species are known to parasitize humans. The condition of being infested with sucking lice is medically referred to as pediculosis. The species Pediculus humanus is further divided into two subspecies. The first, Pediculus humanus humanus, commonly known as the body louse, is sometimes colloquially referred to as the seam squirrel due to its behavior of laying eggs in the seams of clothing. The second subspecies, Pediculus humanus capitis, is known as the head louse and primarily infests the scalp. Another species, Pthirus pubis, commonly referred to as the pubic louse, is responsible for the condition known as crabs.
